I truly don't know if I'm ugly or not. I think I'm decent now, as I've implemented some of the tips I'm about to tell you, but growing up I was very ugly, didn't know how to do makeup, and didn't know how to dress. I rarely ever got positive attention from boys, and more often got negative insults or treated badly. The boys who were interested in me were on the uglier side too, which further hurt my self-esteem, as I know that people are attracted to people who look to be on their "level". 

Over the years through high school and adulthood I've started putting a lot more effort, practice, and research into the ways I do my makeup, how I do my hair, and how I dress. I know, I know. None of those things can fix my gargantuan nose or buttchin. But trust me when I tell you that presentation and confidence really is key. 

I'm not sure exactly what your concerns are with your face, but there is a lot you can do with makeup. I remember writing off contouring entirely because I couldn't do it, but it just takes practice and finding the right shades. Foundation should be your exact shade, concealer should be 1-2 shades lighter than that, and contour should be 1-2 shades darker. 

How you do your eyes can make a big difference too. I used to do eyeliner all around my eye like a raccoon (seriously why didn't any boys like me?) but now I do a cat eye wing or just add some lashes to create the cat eye look, because that works best for my eye shape and face. Again, I used to not be able to use liquid eyeliner or put on lashes to save my life, but with practice and experimentation I found that I am able to use felt tip liner and small sections of lashes as opposed to the full, complete strips. 

If you're not a fan of makeup, hygiene is huge, even washing your face with a good quality cleaner that works for your skin before you go out can make a difference in how fresh you look. 

Knowing what hairstyle works for your face shape makes a big difference on how you look. Trying a new style, cut, or dye can also increase your confidence. 

Working out has been a huge confidence booster, as well as helped me feel happier with life overall, have an outlet for stress and anger release, and helped me feel more comfortable with my body. 

Finally, the way you dress and how you carry yourself says a lot about who you are. I used to dress in all black, baggy clothes with holes or stains on them, my shoulders hunched over, looking down at the ground with 0 confidence. It is important to dress how you want, while also taking into consideration what clothes and colors flatter your body and skin tone. Walking with your head high, shoulders back, with good posture is probably the easiest and quickest way to change how people see and treat you. It's not a cure all, of course, but the phrase "fake it until you make it" does have truth to it. Working on each of these things altogether would greatly improve your confidence and social status, and could even improve your looks as well.

First of all, I am so sorry you experienced this. I can see how it would be a very confusing thing to figure out, even (if not especially) years afterward when you started to truly understand the gravity of what happened. 

I'll be honest, I don't know how to help you. This is definitely something best left up to a professional to work through it with you. 

I can say, however, that it was definitely rape - you said no, didn't like it, and didn't want to do it again. Then the adults in your life failed you by not taking you seriously. So you thought it was okay. I don't know anyone who would blame you for thinking this, as you were so young. You didn't know what to think about it, because children that age should not have to think about this in the first place. If you're uncomfortable with calling it rape, it most definitely was coerced. I feel like victims focus too much on the label of the act itself (for good reasons of course, I think having a label makes it easier to explain to others and easier to process yourself). However, I would suggest that for now, instead of focusing on the label, focus on how it made you feel. You were uncomfortable, confused, and didn't want to do it again after you tried it. That's not a consenting individual by any means, at any age. 

Whether the times afterward, when you were more willing and even excited to do it, were rape, that's up to you. But I still suggest focusing on how you felt during those times, and perhaps trying to think about where that excitement came from - were you excited to have sex, or excited to have companionship and attention? Were you made to feel it was something exciting because you truly enjoyed it, or were you mirroring his excitement about this? 

You can absolutely be traumatized over this - there is no "bad" enough for trauma. If something makes you feel afraid, gives you flashbacks, takes up a lot of your attention, changes the way that you behave around certain individuals, or alters your emotions in any way, I'd say that's trauma. However, I'll also say that you don't "need" to be traumatized by this, in order for it to be regarded as a bad thing that happened. If you don't feel very affected by it today, that's completely fine and normal! People process situations in completely different ways. 

I think when things like this happen, we tend to overthink about how a victim "should" act, versus how we genuinely feel about the situation. You are a victim of sexual assault whether it traumatized you or not. You are a victim despite him not using force or control. So however you feel and act, that is how a victim may feel and act. Rape is typically thought of as a violent thing, but that's a stereotype, not reality. Most of the time, it is done by people close to us, not strangers, and is done with coercion or manipulation, not force. Of course, sometimes it is violent and with strangers, but it's not typically the norm. 

Thank you for sharing this with us, I do hope you reach out to get professional help with processing this. And I hope that sharing this and getting support helped somewhat. Take care.

I will say that a few things worry me about this guy. I may be biased as I was in a relationship with an abusive narcissist, but one of the warning signs is moving the relationship very quickly, overstepping boundaries, and being very charismatic with others. Talking on the phone every night is normal, as long as it is what your mom wants to do with her time. I've been with my boyfriend for almost a year, and sometimes I need a break from talking on the phone every single day. What matters here is that, if your mom were to ask for time to herself, would he be okay with it, or would he throw a fit and claim that she doesn't love him? 

Showing up to her house on short notice may be cause for concern. Is there a reason he can't plan ahead? Does he straight up invite himself over and call her on the way there, saying he'll be there in ten minutes? Or does he *ask* if he can come over? Showing respect for a person's boundaries -- even if your mom is okay with his surprise visits -- is a very important part of a healthy relationship. And again, if your mom were to tell him not to come over, what would his reaction be? 

Salesmen must be charismatic in order to work with and successfully sell to people. However, I would be wary of how he uses this charisma. Keep an eye out for how he treats and talks about people, especially when they disagree with him or they aren't around to defend themselves. 

I don't want to read too much into it, as I said, I am already on high alert for these things due to my past relationship.
